newsitem.title: THAILAND: U.S. calls for Thais to find missing drug suspect.
newsitem.headline: U.S. calls for Thais to find missing drug suspect.

text.p: A man charged in the biggest U.S. heroin seizure in history -- a drug haul worth up to $122 million -- has skipped bail granted by a Thai court, and may now be in Burma out of reach of U.S. and Thai authorities.
The United States said on Tuesday it was deeply concerned by the Thai court's decision to grant bail to Li Yung Chung, also known by the Thai name Phongsak Rogjanasakul.
He was freed on five million baht ($192,308) bail on February 7 by a Thai court and failed to report back on March 7 as ordered, Thai and U.S. officials said.
"The United States is very concerned about the court's action in granting bail to a defendant involved in a major heroin prosecution," a U.S. Embassy spokesman told Reuters.
"We have requested the assistance of the Thai authorities to return Li to custody as soon as possible," he said.
But a Thai drugs official said Li, who has a Thai idendity card but is of Chinese descent, had already fled the country.
"The chances of getting him are very slim since we have information he went to Burma shortly after the court granted him bail," said the official, who asked not to be identified.
Burmese officials could not be reached for comment.

"We are trying to negotiate with the Burmese government," the Thai official said. "If this man was not so important to them they might hand him to us but... the chances are slim. For Khun Sa they had a deal not to extradite him before he surrendered."

Opium warlord Khun Sa, also wanted on drugs charges in the United States, is living in Rangoon after surrendering to Burmese troops last year. Burma has vowed not to extradite him and said the government would deal with him in its own way.

Li was indicted by a New York court in May 1996 in connection with the largest heroin haul ever in the United States -- the seizure in 1991 of 486 kg (nearly 1,070 lb) of the drug in Hayward, California.
Drug officials put the U.S. street value between $180,000 to $250,000 per kg, making the haul worth a whopping $87.5 million to $122 million.

A U.S. government official said investigations by Thai and U.S. officials uncovered enough evidence to indict Li as the principal suspect behind the shipment, thought to be bound for New York from the infamous Golden Triangle region.

The Golden Triangle, where Thailand, Laos and Burma meet, was Khun Sa's home and the region where U.S. drugs officials say about 60 percent of the world's opium -- the raw plant used to produce heroin -- is harvested.

After the indictment was issued, the United States requested Li's extradition from Thailand, the U.S. official said. Under a 1991 extradition treaty between the two countries, narcotics traffickers can be sent to the United States to face trial.
Thai officials arrested Li in July and were holding him for extradition.

"Then we learned he was let out on bail. We don't understand why and are very disappointed," the U.S. official said. "Up until then we had excellent cooperation from Thai authorities, and obviously he is one of the most important drug traffickers."
The Thai narcotics official said police, authorities in the Attorney General's Office and the Office of Narcotics Control Board had repeatedly opposed granting bail for Li.
But bail was eventually granted by a judge, Thai and U.S. officials said.
"There is nothing much we can explain to the U.S., since one cannot interfere in the juridicial process once the case is in the hands of the court," the Thai official said.
